description:
Why Does Neptune's Moon Orbit Backward?

Episode 83 of a daily journey through the universe. 🔄
Triton, Neptune's largest moon: it orbits backward, was probably captured from the Kuiper Belt, and Voyager 2 saw nitrogen geysers there in 1989. Surface around minus 235°C. One day Neptune may tear it apart into rings.

segments.text: Why does one moon go around its planet the wrong way? Triton is a rebel.
Triton is Neptune's biggest moon. And it's a rebel.
segments.headline: Neptune's rebel moon

segments.text: Almost all big moons orbit in the same direction their planet spins. Triton goes the opposite way. Backward.
segments.headline: It orbits backward

segments.text: That suggests it wasn't born there. It was probably a small world from the Kuiper belt, captured by Neptune's gravity.
segments.headline: A captured world

segments.text: Its surface is one of the coldest ever measured: about minus two hundred thirty-five degrees Celsius.
In nineteen eighty-nine, Voyager two flew past and saw something amazing: dark plumes shooting kilometers high. Geysers on an icy moon.
segments.headline: Ice geysers

segments.text: Its surface has a strange pattern, called cantaloupe terrain because it looks like melon skin.
segments.headline: Cantaloupe terrain

segments.text: Triton is slowly spiraling inward. In billions of years, Neptune's gravity may rip it apart.
segments.headline: Spiraling inward

segments.text: Its pieces could form a ring around Neptune, maybe even grander than Saturn's.
